---
title: "Introduction"
bibliography: ../input/bib/jusmer.bib
---

In recent decades, welfare states have undergone significant transformations in their institutional architecture, with social services increasingly  coexisting with private alternatives [@busemeyer_welfare_2020]. As a result, market dynamics have taken root around the world in services such as education, health care, and pension systems. Beyond institucional arrangements, market-oriented policies have not only formal consequences but also cultural ones, operating as  moral projects in which individuals adopt such values as normative criteria [@fourcade_moral_2007]. In this context, the concept of market justice has become key to understanding how people justify the fact that access to and the quality of social services depend on market criteria such as the ability to pay.

Some studies have examined how preferences for market justice relate to structural and cultural characteristics. On the structural side, objective status variables such as education, income, and occupational status have been related to a higher preference for market justice mechanisms, consisten with a rational approach [@lindh_public_2015]. In this area the results are rather inconsistent: while @lindh_public_2015 found that those from a higher social class tend to support market-oriented distribution, [@castillo_justification_2026] found no significant differences between class position and market justice regarding pensions. In this regard, it  one’s position in the social structure does not seem sufficient on its own to account for such beliefs, leading to turn the look to complementary status variables, such as subjective status.

Subjective social status is understood as the self-assessment of one's position within the social hierarchy. In contrast to objective status, it does not imply a categorization of the individual's objective situation, but rather reflects perceived status in terms broader than occupation and income. So far, self-perceived status has played a minor role in the study of market preferences, despite the evidence of its role on perceptions of inequality and the demand for redistribution [@melli_uncovering_2025; @melli_where_2025; @bar-haim_still_2018]. As @hiltner_view_2024 points out, the subjective dimension may provide greater insights into attitudes and behaviors than objective measures. Thus, such perspective can enrich and complement the study of social status and market justice, broadening the explanatory framework of market justice.

The conceptualzation and operationalization of subjective social status has been mostly static. However, there is evidence that challenges this idea; @hiltner_view_2024 argues that the way people perceive their own movement through social hierarchies is more important than their movements within the labor market. In this way, self-perception can also reflect how people assess their trajectories—whether upward or downward—at a given moment, as well as how this perception changes over time. Within this framework, subjective mobility takes on particular significance, as it allows for the study of status in broader terms than occupational attainment—which is used to measure objective mobility—and, along the same lines, can provide greater insights than standardized measures [@duru-bellat_objective_2008; @mijs_belief_2022].

This study aims to contribute to the literature on market justice and social stratification in two ways. First, through a rigorous examination of objective social status and, above all, subjective social status. Our data allows a comprehensive operationalization of subjective status, given that, in addition to one’s own subjective social status, we include that of the family of origin (past) and that of one’s children (future expectation). This allow us generating a series of variables to analytically represent subjective social mobility and consequently observe how they relate to market justice. Secondly, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to address the interaction between objective and subjective social status on market justice preferences and how they change over time. Our main argument is that subjective social status (both cross-sectionally and in terms of mobility) will carry the same or greater weight than objective status, shedding new light on how the perception of one’s own life trajectory plays a fundamental role in market-oriented criteria of justice.

This research is particularly relevant in Chile, a country characterized by a model marked by high levels of inequality and rigid social mobility [@flores_top_2020; @torche_intergenerational_2014], the foundations of which took shape during the civil-military dictatorship that the country endured between 1973 and 1989 [@madariaga_three_2020]. Similarly, there is a high degree of privatization in areas of social reproduction, coupled with a strong dependence on the state [@boccardo_30_2020]. In addition, we have the Chilean Longitudinal Social Survey (ELSOC), a unique project in Latin America that tracked and recorded people’s characteristics and beliefs between 2016 and 2023, allowing us to study change over time. Thus, these conditions make the study of Chile a productive case for understanding the extent to which status (both objective and subjective) determines preferences for market justice.
